66c99cda-25a5-50f2-903b-bfb1fdc5fa10.title: Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials

e-21695.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/d9bdce761076544aff166409cc78bdf918c4afc2c47b67e6366e3aabb78087b7.png)
Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2,$ shown above. Find the fundamental matrix for the system.
e-21695.worked_solution:
Given a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A \mathbf{x},$ where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $\Phi(t)$ of the system is an $n \times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our cases, we have a $2 \times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{5t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{5t} \\ 4{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/bb710709a593f8d185cde601fb5082d7f79ed21af824c28949477d2011479d95.png)

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi$ can be written in any order.

e-21697.knowledge_point: Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix
e-21697.problem:
Consider the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2 \times 2$ matrix. Let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $\Phi(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation $\Phi'(t) = A \, \Phi(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $\big[ \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b} \big]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$*

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_2'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_2(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1'(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2'(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) =  \big[ A \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: A \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \Phi(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/be39ec10432eb81c3e00fdf30599353450e1ae7ebebd136f20dce45deb685cac.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/09febb48bb00d22caebf088103181b5db6377befccad18f1370718351cc91e9d.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L7}$ follows from line $\textrm{L6}$ and substitution from line ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/999db06dcfe0878ddb3316b11546668ba9442d8fd110165e5076b90964b84905.png).
e-21697.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L2}.$ Since $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t).
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that $\mathbf{x}_1$ is a solution of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
\Phi'(t)=\big[A\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:A\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]
= A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by factoring out $A$ on the left.

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L6}$ and $\textrm{L7}.$ From $\textrm{L6}$ we have $\Phi'(t)=A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].$ Using $\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]$ from $\textrm{L1},$ we substitute to obtain $\Phi'(t)=A\Phi(t).$ Thus, $\textrm{L7}$ follows from $\textrm{L6}$ by substitution from $L1.$

e-21696.knowledge_point: Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials
e-21696.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/819e3b9672e898801ef7320c1d80246d218ae89e76b3247c86b642a5f5790400.png)
Consider the system of linear ODEs $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for this system.
e-21696.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0)  = I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -7{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1 = 7\textrm{i}t, \qquad
\lambda_2 = -7\textrm{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((7\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(7\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(7\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+7\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & =7\cdot \frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/4d6fd69672291bf4c39d33a04656258b89a500bc039588a9fd27eb10db328cc3.png)

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
after.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}=[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} & 2t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

decision.explanation: Place the given solutions x₁(t) and x₂(t) as columns to obtain option e. Its determinant is e^{2t}(cos²(2t)+sin²(2t))=e^{2t}, which is nonzero for every t, so it is a fundamental matrix.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
after.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

Given a linear system x′=Ax, where A is an n×n matrix, a fundamental matrix Φ(t) of the system is an n×n matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a 2×2 system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

x1(t)=[cos⁡2tsin⁡2t]et=[etcos⁡2tetsin⁡2t]x2(t)=[−sin⁡2tcos⁡2t]et=[−etsin⁡2tetcos⁡2t]

content.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & {e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

decision.explanation: A fundamental matrix is formed by placing the given solutions x₁(t) and x₂(t) as columns. This gives option c, whose determinant is e^{-2t}(cos²(2t)+sin²(2t))=e^{-2t}, nonzero for every t.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
after.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & {e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

Question 3

x′=[−1−22−1]x,x1(t)=[cos⁡2tsin⁡2t]e−t,x2(t)=[−sin⁡2tcos⁡2t]e−t Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions x1 and x2, shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?

a
[e−1cos⁡2−e−1sin⁡2e−1sin⁡2e−1cos⁡2]
b
[cos⁡2t−sin⁡2tsin⁡2tcos⁡2t]
c
[e−tcos⁡2t−e−tsin⁡2te−tsin⁡2te−tcos⁡2t]
d
[−1−22−1]
e
[e−tcos⁡2te−tsin⁡2t−e−tsin⁡2te−tcos⁡2t]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a linear system x′=Ax, where A is an n×n matrix, a fundamental matrix Φ(t) of the system is an n×n matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a 2×2 system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

x1(t)=[cos⁡2tsin⁡2t]e−t=[e−tcos⁡2te−tsin⁡2t]x2(t)=[−sin⁡2tcos⁡2t]e−t=[−e−tsin⁡2te−tcos⁡2t]

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as Φ(t)=[e−tcos⁡2t−e−tsin⁡2te−tsin⁡2te−tcos⁡2t].

$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
content.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & -{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t & {e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

EXPLANATION

Given a linear system x′=Ax, where A is an n×n matrix, a fundamental matrix Φ(t) of the system is an n×n matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a 2×2 system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

x1(t)=[20]e−t=[2e−t0]x2(t)=[2t1]e−t=[2te−te−t]

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as Φ(t)=[2e−t2te−t0e−t].

Note: The columns of Φ can be written in any order.

content.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}=[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
after.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

a
[cos⁡5t−sin⁡5tsin⁡5tcos⁡5t]
b
[2−552]
c
[e2cos⁡5−e2sin⁡5e2sin⁡5e2cos⁡5]
d
[e2tcos⁡5te2tsin⁡5t−e2tsin⁡5te2tcos⁡5t]
e
[e2tcos⁡5t−e2tsin⁡5te2tsin⁡5te2tcos⁡5t]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a linear system x′=Ax, where A is an n×n matrix, a fundamental matrix Φ(t) of the system is an n×n matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a 2×2 system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

x1(t)=[cos⁡5tsin⁡5t]e2t=[e2tcos⁡5te2tsin⁡5t]x2(t)=[−sin⁡5tcos⁡5t]e2t=[−e2tsin⁡5te2tcos⁡5t]

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as Φ(t)=[e2tcos⁡5t−e2tsin⁡5te2tsin⁡5te2tcos⁡5t].

Note: The columns of Φ can be written in any order.

content.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t & -{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t \\ {e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡5t & {e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡5t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ Line $\text{L1}$ identifies ${x}_{2}(t)$ as a column of $Φ(t),$ so ${x}_{2}(t)$ must satisfy the differential equation. In particular,

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)],$ the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)].
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating each column}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{factoring out }A\text{ on the left}.$

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that Φ(t) satisfies the matrix differential equation Φ′(t)=AΦ(t) is given below.

Hint: [a,b] denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors a and b.

L1: Let Φ(t)=[x1(t),x2(t)]

L2: x1′(t)=Ax1(t)

L3: x2′(t)=Ax2(t)

L4: Φ′(t)=[x1′(t),x2′(t)]

L5: Φ′(t)=[Ax1(t),Ax2(t)]

L6: Φ′(t)=A[x1(t),x2(t)]

L7: Φ′(t)=AΦ(t)

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L3 follows from the fact that Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix and line L1 by the
definition of a fundamental matrix
definition of matrix multiplication
A is diagonalizable
Φ(t) is invertible for all t
definition of a fundamental matrix
.

Line L4 follows from line L1 by
differentiating each column
differentiating each column
multiplying both sides by A
transposing the matrix
factoring out A on the left
.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
factoring out A on the left
transposing the matrix
factoring out A on the left
differentiating again
adding Φ(t) to both sides
.
Submit

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L3. Since Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions of the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t). Line L1 identifies x2(t) as a column of Φ(t), so x2(t) must satisfy the differential equation. In particular, x2′(t)=Ax2(t). Therefore, L3 follows from the fact that Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix and line L1 by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L4. Since Φ(t)=[x1(t),x2(t)], the derivative of Φ(t) is obtained by differentiating each column: Φ′(t)=[x1′(t),x2′(t)]. Thus, L4 follows from L1 by differentiating each column.

  • Finally, we consider lines L5 and L6. We now factor the matrix A on the left: Φ′(t)=[Ax1(t),Ax2(t)]=A[x1(t),x2(t)]. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by factoring out A on the left.

content.knowledge_point: Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix
content.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ Line $\text{L1}$ identifies ${x}_{2}(t)$ as a column of $Φ(t),$ so ${x}_{2}(t)$ must satisfy the differential equation. In particular,

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)],$ the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)].
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating each column}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{factoring out }A\text{ on the left}.$

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from {{field-1}} by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by {{field-4}}.

decision.explanation: L1 identifies the columns of the fundamental matrix, which form a basis of solutions, giving L2. Matrix multiplication gives Φ(t)c=c₁x₁(t)+c₂x₂(t), establishing L4. L3 and L4 equate x(t) and Φ(t)c to the same expression, so L5 follows by transitivity.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from {{field-1}} by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by {{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}$ by the $\text{the transitive property of equality}.$

content.knowledge_point: Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix
content.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from {{field-1}} by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by {{field-4}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}$ by the $\text{the transitive property of equality}.$

after.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ states the independence of the columns of {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ by the {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L2}.$ Line $\text{L2}$ states that the two columns of $Φ(t)$ are linearly independent, which is required of a fundamental matrix. Thus, $\text{L2}$ states independence of the columns of $Φ(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the $\text{properties of invertible matrices}.$

Hint: [a,b] denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors a and b.

L1: Let Φ(t)=[x1(t),x2(t)]

L2: x1′(t)=Ax1(t)

L3: x2′(t)=Ax2(t)

L4: Φ′(t)=[x1′(t),x2′(t)]

L5: Φ′(t)=[Ax1(t),Ax2(t)]

L6: Φ′(t)=A[x1(t),x2(t)]

L7: Φ′(t)=AΦ(t)

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from the fact that
 
x1 is a solution of the system
Φ(t) is invertible for all t
x1 is differentiable
A is diagonalizable
.

Line L5 follows from line L4 and substitution from lines
 
L1 and L3
L2 and L3
L3 and L4
L1 and L2
.

adding Φ(t) to both sides

decision.explanation: L2 holds because x₁ solves x′=Ax. Substituting L2 and L3 into L4 gives L5. Factoring A out on the left gives L6, since [Ax₁, Ax₂]=A[x₁, x₂].

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L2}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{1}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}]=A[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}]=AΦ(t)
$$

Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{factoring out }A\text{ on the left}.$

choices.value: ${x}_{1}$ is a solution of the system

content.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L2}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{1}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}]=A[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}]=AΦ(t)
$$

Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{factoring out }A\text{ on the left}.$

Consider the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant 2×2 matrix. Let Φ(t) be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution x(t) can be written in the form x(t)=Φ(t)c for some constant vector c=[c1,c2]T is given below.

L1: Let x1(t) and x2(t) be the columns of Φ(t)

L2: x1(t) and x2(t) form a basis of solutions

L3: x(t) can be written as x(t)=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L4: Φ(t)c=c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)

L5: x(t)=Φ(t)c

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by the
 
properties of diagonalizable matrices
definition of matrix multiplication
properties of invertible matrices
definition of a fundamental matrix

adding the vectors x1(t) and x2(t)
multiplying Φ(t) with it's inverse
the definition of a basis
integrating the given system

properties of invertible matrices

decision.explanation: The columns of a fundamental matrix form a basis of solutions, giving L2. By the definition of a basis, every solution is a constant linear combination of those columns, giving L3. Matrix multiplication expresses Φ(t)c as that linear combination, giving L4.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:
